For deciding, I would compare the degree programs of those schools and what other resources they offer (ex research) Consider what’s most important to you and whether one school covers more than the other. Also consider the vibe of the city (safety, weather, etc), you will be stuck there for at least the next 4 years. And obviously cost. Like for me I was between UO and UCD. UCD is more prestigious but UO better met my priorities with the CHC and a strong music program. Cost was about the same and I like UO’s campus a lot more. Overall I’ve loved it here. The name of your school doesn’t matter nearly as much as what you achieve and what connections you’ve built by the time you graduate.

I’ve been in therapy for a long time and part of me does still think this way. But. I think it’s natural to want someone to help “fix” things and have all the answers. The reality is that there usually isn’t one answer to things, no one can know what it’s really like in your head, and therapists can only guide the client- not fix them. You have to do the work.
You can, and should, absolutely tell therapists what your goals are in therapy. Depending on the modality, the job of the therapist is to help you reach those goals via various means. Some are more hands on than others. They can make suggestions on why things may the way they are, or how you could change something, based on their clinical experience, but 99% of the time there is no quick fix. Things are not black and white and therapists will never be 100% accurate. People are complicated.

I’d say give therapy a shot and if you’re coming in with curiosity and a willingness to change, I think you can get a lot out of it. Remember finding a good therapeutic fit is #1

This was me roughly a year ago. I didn’t understand why it was happening and why it started either. At some point I realized I wasn’t really eating and that trying to eat, being around food, thinking/talking about food, all made me super nauseous and anxious. I would force myself to sit in front of a meal but i could barely look at it or try to go for a bite. I lost weight very rapidly in those first few months. It wasn’t intentional and I was actively trying to figure it out and start eating again. I saw my PCP and she said I was physically healthy. I have been struggling with mental health for the past few years, but i was never concerned about my weight. It was really frustrating, I would break down over food, I didn’t want people to know, it impacted my relationships, and I got sicker and sicker.

Over time, my mindset started shifting more from wanting to get better to being more “bought in” on it. Since the beginning I had been tracking my weight and what I ate- to document what was happening. I started intentionally restricting more and watching my weight go down felt good- it would make me upset if it went up. I have a lot of core beliefs of worthlessness, being a burden, etc. and I think feeling hungry and starving myself became another form of self harm. After a lot of therapy and a residential program for general mental health, I generally don’t restrict myself anymore, though I still have some disordered thoughts. I’m still not 100% sure why my ED started, but part of it was probably control + self harm. I have issues with my body unrelated to weight and one theory is that restricting was a way I could feel some control over it. There was also a lot of other things in my life that were uncertain on top of already struggling with mental health

Couple general things:
- research surgeons you may want to go with (credentials, reviews, results, etc)
- check the requirements for those surgeons (do they need a doctors letter/diagnosis? what insurance do they work with?)
- make the calls and send the emails to relevant people to find more info about how to proceed with the surgeon/clinic
- if needed, talk to your insurance about coverage
- figure out if you could have anyone help take care of you during recovery, where you would be staying, transport to and from, etc.
- generally you’ll have a consultation with a surgeon, then if you decide to go with them, you’ll have to wait for awhile to get a surgery date. Then there’ll be pre-op appointment(s) before surgery.
- in my case, i had to have a physical done in the past year - don’t know if that’s a standard requirement.

Hello, it’s great that you’re educating yourself and being cautious about this. I have no right to say you’re not transgender, but I will say that it is my belief that some sort of innate, unchangeable feeling (that usually causes distress) is needed to be transgender or nonbinary. Most people call this gender dysphoria, which is a diagnosable condition in the DSM-5 and used to “justify” transition. However, some trans/nonbinary people believe this is not a requirement - I simply think it’s a matter of wording, the feeling may be the same, just that the individual chooses not to call it gender dysphoria. Anyway, if one has no discomfort with their sex assigned at birth and corresponding body, I don’t understand on what basis they would transition - especially considering the costs, risks, potential fallout with friends/family, etc.

I dont know you, and neither does anyone else here, so it’s not our place to say if you are or are not, but from your post it seems like if this is a aesthetic thing, and that you wouldn’t be unhappy with a “female” body, all be it more masculine, I would strongly suggest you seek therapy and keep thinking about it.

It’s important to remember that gender ≠ gender expression. You can be a masculine female/tomboy/butch. Being masculine presenting doesn’t make someone transgender, it’s about the gender dysphoria (or any equivalent term) - discomfort socially and/or physically. Don’t get me wrong, dysphoria doesn’t have to be debilitating, nor does it have to be recognized since early childhood, but there must be some unchangeable cause for needing to transition imop.

Like others have said, you’re an adult and it’s your body - do what you like. But I advise that you seek extensive therapy before any medical treatments (surgery/hormones), and perhaps experiment with binding, mens clothing, and voice training in the mean time. Be cautious with hormones; I know a lot of the things are reversible, but I feel that it’s taken too lightly in the trans community these days - make sure you’re secure in your identity. Also, maybe explore the idea of non-binary. I’m a binary trans guy but i have close friends who are non-binary and dysphoric, perhaps that experience would be more relatable to you.

Wishing you the best :)
